In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects over 90% of adults worldwide, causing infectious mononucleosis (IM) in adolescents and young adults and contributing to multiple malignancies.
Despite its global burden, population-level transmission modeling of EBV remains limited.
We present the first population-level agent-based model (ABM) of EBV transmission.
The model is implemented with 10,000 agents and calibrated to age-specific seroprevalence data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

Two complementary calibration methods are evaluated, each with its own distinct advantages: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) and Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO-EQI).
ABC directly yields an approximate distribution of transmission parameters for propagation through vaccination scenarios.
BO-EQI uses a limited simulation budget to identify well-fitting parameter vectors, particularly as the number of fitted parameters increases.

We estimate parameter uncertainty at each resolution in a separate Gaussian-kernel posterior analysis, which requires additional simulations and an explicit model for discrepancies between simulated and observed prevalence.
As an illustrative application, we simulate the population-level effect of hypothetical EBV vaccines over a 100-year projection horizon.

Similar to a previous modeling study, our results suggest that vaccine durability is at least as critical as efficacy, and that a vaccine with direct protection against only EBV may persistently shift IM burden to older ages, an effect our longer simulation horizon reveals to be a durable equilibrium shift rather than a transient cohort phenomenon.

These findings highlight the importance of careful vaccine target product profile design; in particular, our results suggest that dual efficacy against both EBV infection and IM progression represents the most promising achievable target profile, and should be a core design objective for next-generation EBV vaccines.
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is one of the most widespread human pathogens, with seroprevalence exceeding 90% in adults worldwide 1, 2 .

text.text: Primary infection usually occurs in childhood, where it is often asymptomatic, but acquisition during adolescence or early adulthood frequently results in infectious mononucleosis (IM) 3 .

text.text: Following infection, commonly through saliva 4 , EBV establishes latency within B cells and can periodically reactivate, leading to viral shedding and continued opportunities for transmission 1 .

text.text: Beyond illness, EBV has been shown to result in several malignancies, including multiple sclerosis (MS), Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL), nasopharyngeal cancer and gastric cancer [5] [6] [7] .

text.text: Despite its global burden, the transmission dynamics of EBV is not as thoroughly studied as those of other common viruses like influenza.
The difficulty arises from asymptomatic infections, heterogeneous shedding, and the challenge of measuring interpersonal contacts relevant for transmission.
Over the decades, attempts to control EBV infection and its sequelae have focused on managing symptoms of IM, suppressing viral replication, and preventing EBV-driven malignancies.
Antiviral therapies such as acyclovir, ganciclovir, and valganciclovir have been trialed, primarily targeting lytic replication [8] [9] [10] .

text.text: Lytic replication, or the lytic cycle, is a viral reproduction process where a virus infects a host cell, replicates its genetic material, and ultimately destroys the host cell to release new viral particles.

While these drugs can reduce viral shedding in the short term, clinical studies have shown little benefit in altering the course of infectious mononucleosis or preventing latency, since EBV persists as an episome within B cells 11 .

text.text: Similarly, corticosteroids have been used to manage severe IM complications such as airway obstruction, but they are not recommended for routine treatment due to limited benefit and potential risks 12 .

text.text: These results highlight the challenge of intervening after primary infection has occurred.
Vaccination against EBV has long been considered an attractive preventive strategy, particularly given its contribution to both acute morbidity and long-term cancer risk.

The most advanced vaccine candidate to date was a recombinant glycoprotein (gp) 350 subunit vaccine developed by GlaxoSmithKline Biologicals (Rixensart, Belgium), which was tested in a large phase 2 trial.
This vaccine reduced the incidence of IM by 78% (95% CI [1.0% -96.0%]) but did not prevent EBV infection itself 13 .

text.text: More recently, efforts have shifted toward vaccines targeting multiple viral antigens, including those involved in viral entry into epithelial and B cells 14 .
text.formatted: More recently, efforts have shifted toward vaccines targeting multiple viral antigens, including those involved in viral entry into epithelial and B cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: Advances in nanoparticle platforms and mRNA technologies have renewed interest in EBV vaccine development, with several candidates currently in preclinical or early clinical stages 15, 16 .

text.text: These approaches aim not only to reduce IM but also to mitigate downstream risks of EBV-associated cancers and autoimmune diseases.
Mathematical modeling offers a valuable framework, allowing exploration of how age structure, infection outcomes, and behavioral factors shape population-level patterns of EBV spread.

Such models also provide tools to test hypothetical scenarios such as vaccination programs, which are increasingly under consideration given the morbidity associated with IM and EBV's role in cancer risk.
Previous research on EBV transmission modeling has employed diverse approaches to understand infection dynamics and inform public health strategies.
Goscé et  al.  (2019) 17 represents the most comprehensive population-level mathematical model of EBV transmission to date, explicitly incorporating age structure and vaccination scenarios.

The study also noted that vaccinating younger age groups could unintentionally delay infection to later ages, thereby increasing the likelihood of IM.

The agent based model we develop also uses this data.
In this study, we develop a flexible, long-horizon agent-based model of EBV transmission and IM development.
It is the first agent-based model, and only the second population-level transmission model 17 of EBV.
text.formatted: It is the first agent-based model, and only the second population-level transmission model <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> of EBV.

text.text: The first model, a compartmental model, was parametrized using data from England.
The agent-based model we develop is calibrated with data from the United States.

An agent-based model was chosen over a compartmental one in order to facilitate the simulation of heterogeneous populations, and to allow the tracking of complex individual health state histories (e.g. age at EBV infection and IM onset) without requiring a combinatorial explosion in the number of compartments.
Being able to resolve these histories in detail is critical to the future addition of EBV-associated sequelae, e.g.
MS.

We also use this model as a testbed for comparing two calibration strategies for stochastic agent-based models: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) and Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO-EQI).
We distinguish point calibration from uncertainty quantification.
ABC directly supplies a joint parameter sample for the vaccination projections.
BO-EQI directs simulations toward finding a well-fitting point under a fixed evaluation budget.
We additionally examine parameter uncertainty through a separate importance-sampled posterior; its intervals are not an output of BO-EQI itself.
Finally, we use the calibrated model to examine illustrative 2/28 hypothetical vaccine scenarios selected to be comparable with previous EBV modeling work.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 describes the agent-based model framework.

Sections 3 and 4 present two methods of calibration for the estimation of the probability of transmission per meaningful contact in the agent based model of EBV infection: the Approximate Bayesian Calibration (ABC) method and Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO-EQI) algorithm.
Section 5 presents the outcomes observed when vaccination against EBV is introduced, for different target product profiles.
Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.
We developed an agent-based model implemented in R to study the transmission of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and the occurrence of Infectious Mononucleosis (IM) within a synthetic population.

At initialization, the model generates a population of agents distributed across age and sex-assigned-at-birth to reflect the demographic structure of the target setting, with some agents seeded as EBV-infected.
The demographic structure of the model is informed by population birth rates 21 and age-stratified mortality rates 22 .

The probability of EBV transmission per infectious contact is calibrated using as the target the age-specific prevalence of EBV within the US population 3 , estimated using data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination (NHANES) survey.

text.text: Time advances in discrete steps; through experimentation, we found that a step size of 28 days adequately resolves the (relatively slow) EBV transmission dynamics.

At each step, agents undergo deterministic changes (aging, waning of protection if vaccinated), and depending on their current state, may probabilistically undergo transitions to vaccinated, infected (EBV or EBV+IM), or death.
This structure allows the simulation to capture how demographic processes, infection risk, and vaccination strategies shape EBV prevalence and IM incidence over time.
The social contact matrix governs exposure opportunities by defining the frequency of interactions between age groups, which drives the probability of transmission.
Upon exposure, susceptible individuals may acquire EBV infection.
If infection occurs, an age-dependent probability governs whether the agent develops IM.
Thus, an agent's health state can be (i) EBV-seronegative; (ii) EBV-seropositive without IM at primary infection; or (iii) EBV-seropositive with IM at primary infection.
The model can optionally be set to demographically rebalance the population at specified intervals.

To minimize any impact of this procedure on transmission dynamics, the infection status of newly introduced agents is sampled from the current age-specific EBV prevalence, thus preserving the age-specific proportion of infectious individuals.
This demographic rebalance is done to maintain the initial population structure as the model is simulated to reach a stable epidemiological state before analyses.
The simulation period during which the model reaches a stable state is known as the warm-up period.

One key challenge in calibrating ABMs is their stochastic behavior: the model produces different outcomes even with the same parameter values, due to random seed variation or probabilistic rules in agent interactions.
Our approach addresses this by using a Bayesian optimization framework tailored for noisy outputs.
In particular, we employ an acquisition function known as Expected Quantile Improvement (EQI) 27 .

text.text: The EQI criterion is a variant of the widely used Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition, modified to handle uncertainty in the output.
EQI uses a GP predictive quantile to evaluate the expected improvement from an additional noisy simulation.
Here the quantile describes uncertainty in the GP prediction of discrepancy.
It does not directly describe the distribution of repeated ABM outcomes or provide uncertainty intervals for the infection parameters.

Vaccination was handled as a one-time opportunity upon an agent reaching the eligible age, using an uptake of 80% across all scenarios.
We considered three vaccination ages (1, 5, or 11 years), two vaccine efficacies (80% or 100%), and either lifelong protection or waning protection.
In the waning scenario, efficacy was assumed to decline exponentially such that, 15 years after vaccination, it remained at 80% of its initial value.

text.text: In most scenarios, the vaccine was implemented as being efficacious only against EBV, as in the model of Goscé et al.; no direct efficacy against IM was modeled.
However, we also considered a set of scenarios with a vaccine having dual efficacies of 80% against both EBV and IM, both with a 15-year duration of protection.
Results are shown in figures Figures 9 to 14.

Since IM is an acute (rather than lifelong) condition with highly variable duration, and to align with how real-world IM burden is usually reported, we show the incidence rather than the prevalence for IM.

We observe that the relative impact of vaccine efficacy versus duration changes with age group: Below age 25, increasing efficacy from 80% to 100% achieves roughly the same reduction after 100 years as increasing duration of protection from 15 years to lifetime, whereas in the 25+ group, increase in duration has the greater effect.
We also see that for a given efficacy and duration, earlier vaccination achieves greater EBV reduction.
In the case of lifetime protection, the reason is simple: Earlier vaccination means fewer years exposed to infection before becoming protected.
However, in the case of waning protection, there is a competing effect: Earlier vaccination means earlier waning.
Across our scenarios, the former effect is evidently stronger than the latter.
More diverse behavior becomes apparent when we look at vaccine impact on the burden of IM.

The "perfect vaccine" scenario (100% efficacy, lifetime protection) remains relatively straightforward; IM incidence is reduced across all age groups below 25, and above 25, where the incidence is already extremely low, it has negligible effect.

Furthermore, all scenarios achieved significant reduction in IM incidence in the highest-incidence 12-18 age group, and waning-protection scenarios showed the strongest impact when vaccination took place just before, at age 11, thus minimizing the effect of waning.
However, above age 18, the picture becomes more complex.
When vaccinating at age 1, all but the perfect vaccine and dual-efficacy scenarios actually increased the IM incidence in the 19-24 age group, by deferring infection to higher ages.
Waning further exacerbated this effect by leaving older ages progressively less protected.
This effect weakened with increasing vaccination age; when vaccinating at age 11, all but the 80%/15yr scenario reduced incidence relative to the baseline.
However, above age 25, all except the perfect vaccine scenario eventually produced elevated IM incidence.
Throughout, the dual-efficacy scenario achieved the second-best protection after the perfect vaccine scenario.

This consistency is important to ensure that θ 1 , θ 2 and θ 3 are collectively a good fit to the observed EBV prevalence data.
In the age range 0-5, all baseline categories overlap.

In this paper, we developed an agent-based model (ABM) of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) transmission that tracks infection dynamics within a synthetic population over many decades.

By incorporating demographic structure, contact patterns, and age-dependent infection processes, the model provides a flexible framework for examining EBV epidemiology beyond standard compartmental approaches.
Calibration to age-specific prevalence data from the United States allowed the simulations to be broadly aligned with available empirical evidence.
To our knowledge, this is only the second transmission model of EBV, and the first agent-based model.
It is also the first model calibrated to the United States.
A key focus of this work was the comparison of two calibration strategies for estimating the probability of EBV infection per meaningful contact.

Using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC), we showed how a large ensemble of simulations can be used to obtain a posterior distribution of infection probabilities that provides a good fit to observed prevalence patterns.
This likelihood-free approach offers a practical way to account for stochasticity and uncertainty in the model, and naturally yields probability distributions for calibrated parameters.

However, there are computational limitations of ABC, particularly as the number of calibrated parameters or the dimensionality of the problem increases, at which point the approach becomes computationally intractable.
In the present work, only three transmission parameters required calibration, corresponding to the three age strata in the Balfour et al. data.

Had we instead stratified the population by race/ethnicity group as Balfour et al. suggest -given that EBV prevalence varies substantially across such groups 3 -we would have required nine parameters simultaneously, at which point ABC becomes prohibitively expensive.
This represents both the natural use case for BO-EQI and an important direction for future work.
To address the scalability limitations of ABC, we explored Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO-EQI) as an alternative calibration strategy.

By formulating calibration as an optimization problem, BO-EQI was able to identify infection probability estimates that reproduce the observed data well while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations.
A tradeoff is that BO-EQI yields parameter point estimates rather than probability distributions.
At the three-parameter level, BO-EQI and ABC yielded closely comparable results, validating both approaches.
At higher dimensionalities, BO-EQI remained tractable where ABC did not, demonstrating its practical value for more biologically detailed parameterizations of heterogeneous populations.
Our vaccination scenario results confirm and extend the findings of Goscé et al. 17 .
text.formatted: Our vaccination scenario results confirm and extend the findings of Goscé et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: Consistent with their compartmental model, we find that vaccine durability is at least as important as efficacy in driving reductions in EBV prevalence, and that earlier vaccination achieves greater reduction in EBV burden across the population.
We also replicate their observation that vaccination can unintentionally shift the IM burden to older ages.
Our results go further, however, in revealing that this is not merely a transient cohort effect.

Over Goscé et al.'s 27-year horizon, it was not possible to determine whether elevated IM incidence at older ages would eventually fade away, or whether it represented a durable shift in the endemic equilibrium.

Our 100-year projections show clearly that it is the latter: even a century after vaccination introduction, scenarios with waning protection continue to exhibit elevated IM incidence at higher ages relative to the unvaccinated baseline.
This persistence reflects the ongoing recycling of susceptible individuals as vaccine protection wanes in each successive cohort.
Our results also illuminate a fundamental vaccine design constraint.
The very property that makes infant vaccination most effective for EBV control -intervening before first exposure -simultaneously maximizes the age-deferral effect on IM.
Vaccinating at age 1 produces the greatest reduction in EBV prevalence across all age groups, but also produces the greatest increase in IM incidence at higher ages.
This tradeoff weakens but does not disappear as vaccination age increases: even at age 11, waning-protection scenarios eventually produce elevated IM incidence above age 25.
The implication is that optimizing a vaccine solely for EBV infection prevention, without regard to what happens to deferred infections, risks a net increase in IM morbidity at the population level.
This observation motivated our dual-efficacy scenario, and connects directly to the history of EBV vaccine development.
The most clinically advanced candidate to date, the gp350/AS04 subunit vaccine 13 , demonstrated approximately 78% efficacy against IM but no efficacy against EBV infection itself.
text.formatted: The most clinically advanced candidate to date, the gp350/AS04 subunit vaccine <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , demonstrated approximately 78% efficacy against IM but no efficacy against EBV infection itself.

text.text: Conversely, a vaccine with efficacy only against EBV infection reduces transmission and prevalence but does not protect breakthrough-infected individuals from developing IM.
Our dual-efficacy scenario is, to our knowledge, the first modelling analysis to quantify what happens when both components act in tandem.

The results are clear: across all vaccination ages, the dual-efficacy profile consistently achieves the second-best IM outcomes after the biologically implausible "perfect" vaccine, substantially outperforming EBV-only vaccination at ages 19 and above.
This finding argues that dual efficacy against both EBV infection and IM progression should be treated as a core component of future EBV vaccine target product profiles.
The recent shift toward mRNA and nanoparticle platforms 15, 16 , which offer greater design flexibility than earlier subunit approaches, makes this goal increasingly realistic.

text.text: Several limitations of the present analysis warrant acknowledgement.
First, the probabilities of developing infectious mononucleosis (IM) following primary EBV infection were estimated from Danish registry data covering ages up to 29 years 20 .
text.formatted: First, the probabilities of developing infectious mononucleosis (IM) following primary EBV infection were estimated from Danish registry data covering ages up to 29 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Beyond that age, we assume that these probabilities remain constant at their age-29 values.
In subsection 5.2, we investigate the impact of declining this probability.
The magnitude of the increase in IM incidence in the 25+ age group is lower if the probability is assumed to decrease.

However, whether the probability of IM upon primary EBV infection remains high, declines, or approaches zero in middle age is not well established empirically, particularly in the hypothetical setting of vaccination-deferred infection.
The probability of EBV infection per meaningful contact is calibrated to observed data from the US NHANES for ages 6-19.
This data is used to calibrate the probabilities across the entire population based on how well the parameters fit to the available observed data.
The sensitivity of the parameter representing the 0-5 age group is explored in subsection 5.3.
Nationally representative seroprevalence studies in children aged 0-5 years could better constrain early-life transmission parameters.
Also, as noted above, the pooling of all race/ethnicity groups into a single calibration may limit results.

Balfour et al. 3 document variations in EBV seroprevalence across racial and ethnic groups in the United States, and a calibration that treated these groups separately would have different transmission parameters (a higher number of parameters) which could provide population dynamics closer to the real world for analysis.
text.formatted: Balfour et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> document variations in EBV seroprevalence across racial and ethnic groups in the United States, and a calibration that treated these groups separately would have different transmission parameters (a higher number of parameters) which could provide population dynamics closer to the real world for analysis.

text.text: In addition to that, our model does not capture the intermittent and highly variable 31 nature of EBV shedding by infected individuals.
text.formatted: In addition to that, our model does not capture the intermittent and highly variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> nature of EBV shedding by infected individuals.

text.text: We abstract infectiousness as a constant average value.
Other biological complexities that may influence EBV transmission and disease outcomes include vital strain diversity, co-infections and variation in mucosal immunity.
Excluding these mechanisms may limit the model's ability to capture heterogeneity in susceptibility and infectiousness.

Finally, although ABC provides posterior distributions that capture uncertainty, it has high computational cost which increases as the number of calibrated parameters and the population size grows, limiting its practicality for models with higher stratification.
BO-EQI addresses this computational challenge and remains tractable at higher dimensions, but at the cost of returning point estimates rather than probability distributions of parameters.
Despite these limitations, this study provides both a methodological framework and substantive epidemiological findings that are relevant to EBV vaccine development.

The ABM architecture, with its ability to track complete individual infection histories, is particularly well-suited to the addition of downstream sequelae such as multiple sclerosis and Hodgkin's lymphoma in future work, outcomes for which the age at primary EBV infection, and its interaction with vaccination, may be of direct clinical importance.

For vaccine development and public health planning, model findings could also be translated into clearer target product profiles that distinguish vaccines designed primarily to prevent EBV infection from those that additionally reduce the risk of infectious mononucleosis, including explicit consideration of efficacy, durability of protection, and age at vaccination.
